blocks.content: {{term:doe|Design of Experiments}} (DoE) plans experiments so that maximum insight about several factors is gained from as few runs as possible. While the classical "one factor at a time" approach needs many runs and misses interactions, DoE delivers structured designs that efficiently separate {{term:haupteffekt|main effects}} and {{term:wechselwirkung|interactions}}.
A {{term:faktor|factor}} is an input deliberately varied — e.g. temperature, pressure, time, material type. Factors can be continuous (temperature in °C) or categorical (supplier A/B).

{{term:stufe|Levels}} are the concrete values a factor is set to in the experiment. 2 levels (−1 / +1) are standard for {{term:screening-design|screening}}, 3+ levels for optimization (e.g. response surface).
The {{term:zielgroesse|response}} is the output to optimize or understand — e.g. yield, strength, cycle time. Measured once per run.
A {{term:vollfaktoriell|full factorial}} tests all combinations of all levels. With k factors at 2 levels: 2ᵏ runs. Exact but quickly expensive (6 factors = 64 runs).

A {{term:teilfaktoriell|fractional factorial}} is a deliberately chosen fraction of the full design — e.g. a half (2ᵏ⁻¹) or quarter. Efficient for screening many factors, but specific interactions become {{term:konfundierung|confounded (aliased)}}.

In an {{term:wechselwirkung|interaction}}, two factors do not act independently — the effect of A depends on the level of B. Detecting interactions is one of DoE's main benefits; they are entirely missed in the "one factor at a time" world.
{{term:zentralpunkt|Center points}} are run(s) at the center of the design region (all factors at 0). Checks for curvature and estimates pure variation.

In {{term:streuungs-doe|dispersion DoE}} — designs with at least two replicates per point — the planner additionally fits a model for ln(s²). This identifies factor settings that reduce process variability independently of the {{term:mittelwert|mean}} — shown in the analysis section below the design quality summary.

DoE is the hardest weapon of the Improve phase — if you don't know which factors matter, a screening design answers in a few runs. If you already know your factors and want to optimize, use response-surface designs.

The left side lists the factors with unit, kind and levels, and the responses below. Continuous factors have numbers as levels, categorical ones names. Once factors, responses and design type are complete, the design is built by itself after about a second.

The recommendation suggests a type by factor count and levels. Fractional factorials choose a cell of the resolution table, Plackett-Burman a design, Taguchi an array; optimal designs (D, A, G) choose model terms and run count and can forbid factor combinations or build on runs already measured in a worksheet.

The right side shows the preview of the design; values entered there go into the datasheet when it is created. Afterwards the results are entered in the datasheet, and the planner shows how far it is filled. When the design changes, the datasheet is outdated and can be recreated. Only actual configuration changes discard the design; clicking the active design type again or entering the same run count changes nothing.

Efficiency, VIF, alias structure and power rate the design before the experiment. With replicates the dispersion analysis shows which factors affect the spread; once all results are in, a button hands the datasheet to a regression.

In project mode the design becomes the first phase. Once its results are in, you decide: recenter (around the best run), repeat or stop. The timeline shows all phases; a click brings a phase back with its design and datasheet.
Hold Alt to show question marks at headings, column heads and buttons; a click explains the element.

“Reshuffle”: The plan is generated with a fixed seed — the same configuration always yields the same plan, including the run order. “Reshuffle” draws a new run order (new seed) without changing the configuration.

items: Clearly define the response — what should be optimized or understood?
Pick factors and sensible levels — with process experts, not at the desk.
Identify noise variables to be held constant or randomized.
Choose a design type: screening (Plackett-Burman, fractional 2ᵏ⁻ᵖ), optimization (response surface, central composite), mixtures.
Randomize — run order random, not systematic.
Run the experiments, measure the response, record data carefully.
Fit the model, assess main effects and interactions.
Confirm with runs at the predicted best settings.

blocks.content: Running experiments in the standard-table order confounds factor effects with drift over time (tool wear, temperature change). {{term:randomisierung|Randomization}} is mandatory, not optional.
When levels sit close together, the effect hides in the noise. Be bold with wide levels — they need only stay meaningful, not "safe".

blocks.term: Too many factors, too little knowledge
blocks.content: Studying 10 factors at once yields a huge design and little time per effect. Rule of thumb: prior knowledge and prioritization first, DoE second — not the other way around.

A half-fractional design confounds certain main effects with interactions. Before analyzing, inspect the {{term:konfundierung|alias structure}} and {{term:aufloesung|resolution}}, otherwise conclusions will be wrong.
A single value per condition provides no noise estimate. Use at least two {{term:replikat|replicates}} or center points, otherwise pure variation remains unknown.
The found optimum is a prediction — until it is run on the real process, it is just an equation. Confirmation runs are the decisive final step.
The model applies inside the studied region. Predictions outside (e.g. even higher temperature than ever tested) are pure speculation.
